facts.statement: The genus Cryptoclidus was described by Seeley in 1892.
The name Cryptoclidus means "hidden clavicles" because the animal possessed small, nearly invisible collar bones buried in its shoulder girdle.
facts.quote: Its name, meaning "hidden clavicles", refer to its small, practically invisible clavicles buried in its front limb girdle.

facts.statement: The specific name "eurymerus" means "wide femur," a name given because the forelimb was originally mistaken for a hindlimb.
facts.quote: The specific name "wide femur" refers to the forelimb, which was mistaken for a hindlimb at the time.

facts.statement: Cryptoclidus lived during the Middle Jurassic to Late Jurassic periods, specifically from the Callovian to the Oxfordian stages.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Middle Jurassic to Late Jurassic (Callovian to Oxfordian)

facts.statement: Cryptoclidus fossils have been found in England, France, and Cuba.
facts.quote: Cryptoclidus ( ) is a genus of plesiosaur reptile from the Middle Jurassic period of England, France, and Cuba.

facts.statement: The largest known individuals of Cryptoclidus measured up to 4 meters in length and weighed between 737 and 756 kilograms.
facts.quote: Cryptoclidus was a medium-sized plesiosaur, with the largest individuals measuring up to 4 m long and weighing about 737 - 756 kg.

facts.statement: Cryptoclidus adapted to marine life by transforming its limbs into long, narrow flippers.
facts.quote: Este reptil oceánico se readaptó a la vida en el mar mediante la transformación de sus extremidades en aletas largas y estrechas.

facts.statement: Recent discoveries indicate that the bone structure of its trunk allowed Cryptoclidus to live only in the water.
facts.quote: Sin embargo se ha descubierto recientemente que la estructura ósea de su tronco solo le habría permitido vivir en el agua.

facts.statement: The time range for Cryptoclidus is estimated to be from 165.3 to 143.1 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Callovian to Tithonian (165.3 to 143.1 million years ago)

facts.statement: Cryptoclidus belongs to the family Cryptoclididae.
Cryptoclidus is classified within the subfamily Cryptoclidinae.
The type species of Cryptoclidus was initially described as Plesiosaurus eurymerus.
facts.quote: The type species was initially described as Plesiosaurus eurymerus.

facts.statement: Fossils of Cryptoclidus have been found in the Oxford Clay of Cambridgeshire, England.
facts.quote: Fossils of Cryptoclidus have been found in the Oxford Clay of Cambridgeshire, England.

facts.statement: The dubious species Cryptoclidus beaugrandi is known from Kimmeridgian-age deposits in Boulogne-sur-Mer, France.
facts.quote: The dubious species Cryptoclidus beaugrandi is known from Kimmeridgian-age deposits in Boulogne-sur-Mer, France.

facts.statement: The species Cryptoclidus vignalensis, now considered undiagnostic, comes from the Jagua Formation of western Cuba.
facts.quote: Cryptoclidus vignalensis, which is now considered undiagnostic, hails from the Jagua Formation of western Cuba.

facts.statement: A 2016 report described a fragmentary Cryptoclidus skeleton from Russia, but later research defined it as an intermediate cryptoclidid.
facts.quote: In 2016, there was a report about a fragmentary Cryptoclidus postcranial skeleton from the Callovian deposits of Nikitino village in Spassky District, Ryazan Oblast, Russia, but later Zverkov et al. defined it as an intedermitate cryptoclidid.

facts.statement: Fossils of Cryptoclidus have been found in the Oxford Clay (England), Boulogne-sur-Mer (France), Lajas Formation (Argentina), and Jagua Formation (Cuba).
facts.quote: Se han encontrado fósiles de Cryptoclidus en: Oxford Clay, Inglaterra Boulogne-sur-Mer, Francia Formación de Lajas, Neuquén Basin, Argentina Formación de Jagua, Cuba

facts.statement: It is debated whether a specific Russian fossil fragment belongs to Cryptoclidus or represents an intermediate form between Cryptoclidus and other cryptoclidids.
facts.quote: In 2016, there was a report about a fragmentary Cryptoclidus postcranial skeleton from the Callovian deposits of Nikitino village in Spassky District, Ryazan Oblast, Russia, but later Zverkov et al. defined it as an intedermitate cryptoclidid.
